expert_opinion.location: Results, lines 1918-1926 (see also Methods lines 1453-1505; Discussion lines 2193-2201; References lines 2483-2487)
expert_opinion.quote:
We also tested the hypothesis that children with DLD were less likely in the QHP task to 

reach across the midline with the right hand to a spatial position on the left side of the body, 

indicating weaker hand preference, as previously reported (Bishop, 2005; E. L. Hill & Bishop, 

1998). A multilevel model was run with twin pair membership as a random effect, group as a 

between factor and spatial position as a within factor.
expert_opinion.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work (never previously adjudicated). The source text explicitly re-tests the finding of Bishop (2005) (doi:10.1002/dev.20062) that developmental language disorder (SLI/DLD) is associated with a reduced tendency to reach across the midline with the right hand on the Quantification of Hand Preference (QHP) task. This empirical replication test is specified in Methods (lines 1453-1505), executed via multilevel modeling in Results (lines 1918-1960), and evaluated in the Discussion (lines 2193-2201). It is an independent original study (6-year-old twins in Developmental Psychobiology) distinct from shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008, adult fTCD cerebral dominance) and from sibling target 1 (Hill & Bishop, 1998, clinical SLI/DCD sample in Laterality).

corrected_value.authors: Illingworth, S., & Bishop, D. V. M.
corrected_value.title: Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound

expert_opinion.location: Conclusions, lines 2385-2395 (see also Methods lines 1281-1295; Discussion lines 2183-2189; References lines 2869-2875)
expert_opinion.quote:
In a large sample of twins oversampled for language problems, the present study failed to 

find evidence for atypical laterality, either in terms of handedness or cerebral lateralisation for 

language, in those with DLD. Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left 

hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems 

(e.g. Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; T. J. Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small 

samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008).
expert_opinion.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. In Methods (lines 1281-1295), the authors explicitly include children impaired on literacy measures in the DLD group on the basis of Illingworth & Bishop's (2009) fTCD finding of reduced left-hemisphere language lateralisation in dyslexia, and in both the Discussion (lines 2183-2189) and Conclusions (lines 2385-2415) they explicitly state that their fTCD comparison failed to replicate the reduced left-hemisphere language dominance reported by Illingworth & Bishop (2009) (doi:10.1016/j.bandl.2009.05.002) and Whitehouse & Bishop (2008). Because shipped row 2411 captures only Whitehouse & Bishop (2008) (blind target 3), Illingworth & Bishop (2009) is a genuinely distinct missing replication target.

source_evidence.quote: The goals of the present study included (1) replication of identifying a pattern of dysregulated fear in toddlers (Buss, 2011) in a new sample; (2) replication of the prediction from toddler dysregulated fear to elevated social inhibition (Buss, 2011; Buss et al., 2013); and (3) extending our understanding of the implications of dysregulated fear for children’s development by linking this pattern of high fearfulness in low-threat contexts to physiological reactivity as a putative psychophysiological marker of dysregulated emotion processes in toddlerhood. Results were largely consistent with expectations—we were able to replicate the identification of children with dysregulated fear in this new sample, showed that this pattern of fear responding predicted inhibition across early childhood, and identified modest evidence for the idea that children who manifest a dysregulated fear pattern of behavior would also show a distinct pattern of physiological responding to laboratory challenges.

source_evidence.role: cohort continuity and differentiated follow-up findings
source_evidence.quote: To examine this possibility, Buss (2011) assessed fear behavior of N = 111 toddlers across novel situations (e.g., modified from the Lab-TAB) that ranged from putatively low-threat contexts that pulled for engagement and pleasure (e.g., Puppet Show) to putatively high-threat contexts that pulled for withdrawal and displeasure (e.g., Spider). The pattern of fear was modeled as both a continuous variable, representing the slope of fear ‘intensity’ across the tasks ordered from low to high threat where a flatter slope represented greater dysregulation of fear; and as latent profiles where two distinct patterns of fear behavior emerged. Most toddlers (90% of sample) exhibited a normative fear profile, characterized by context appropriate fear behavior – low levels of fear behavior in low-threat situations and higher levels of fear behavior in high-threat situations. In contrast, a small group of toddlers (10% of sample) exhibited a dysregulated fear profile characterized by context inappropriate fear behavior – high levels of fear in both the low-threat and high-threat situations. Tracked for four years, dysregulated fear was associated with greater social withdrawal (Buss, 2011) throughout the preschool years and kindergarten, as well as social anxiety disorder symptoms (Buss et al., 2013) at 6 years, compared to a more normative fear profile.

source_evidence.quote: To confirm that fear sensitivity was associated with greater social inhibition, we examined the correlations between fear sensitivity and parent-reported inhibition to novelty obtained at 24- and 36- months, and social inhibition obtained at 48-months. Results are summarized in Table 1. At all three ages, fear sensitivity was associated with inhibition ratings such that greater dysregulation in fear was associated with higher scores on parent-reported inhibition.

records.label: objection
records.reason: The duplicate exclusion is not established sufficiently for context approval. The paper expressly names Buss (2013), together with Buss (2011), for replication of dysregulated fear predicting elevated social inhibition and executes that relationship in a new cohort. It also documents a shared earlier cohort and distinguishes preschool withdrawal from later social-anxiety findings. Thus cohort continuity is real, but does not by itself show that the 2013 published follow-up finding is only another report of the exact 2011 finding. No age-six diagnostic endpoint is measured here; that limits the retest to the social-inhibition relation and does not exclude a conceptual retest. Corrected row 418 is Buss (2011), while shipped Phelps (2016) and its 2015 preliminary EEG citation are current-sample biomarker work. The earlier/current adjudication expressly retained Buss (2013); its malformed payload is not evidence that the scientific relationship was wrong. Parent must resolve report equivalence against that explicit prior inclusion and the one-entry-per-original-paper codebook rule.
